newsitem.title: DUBAI: Three-year-old Qatar Airways goes for relaunch.
newsitem.headline: Three-year-old Qatar Airways goes for relaunch.

text.p: Three-year-old Qatar Airways is being relaunched with a new corporate image and livery to help widen its appeal to first and business class passengers from its mainstay, budget travellers, its senior general manager said.
"We are turning our airline around in 20 weeks," Michael Hewitt told a news conference in Dubai on Tuesday on the sidelines of the annual Arabian Travel Market exhibition.

"We are repositioning ourselves to take advantage of the market in Qatar and the lower Gulf to offer a product that will appeal to wealthy Qataris, Gulf nationals and first world corporate travellers, in addition to expanding our India and Philippines service."
Until now, most of its customers have been labourers from the Indian subcontinent who come to work in the oil-rich Gulf.
The new logo is what Hewitt called a refined version of the old maroon and grey oryx.

The relaunch would involve a total refurbishment of the airline's eight aircraft. Last month's 70 million riyal ($19 million) interest-free government loan would help finance the modernisation and growth plan, Hewitt said.
It would also help pay for the upgrading of the Doha cargo terminal and ground handling and catering facilities.

The airline would expand its network of some 30 destinations, including introducing daily flights to Heathrow and doubling capacity to India, and offer in-flight video entertainment and alcohol on board from June.
Alcohol consumption is banned by Islam and restricted in most Gulf states.
"Last year we carried just under 450,000 passengers, and this year we are looking for something like 800,000 and the following year 1.5 million passengers," Hewitt said.

The airline -- 70 percent owned by the Qatar ruling family, with the foreign minister as its chairman -- dismissed its chief executive and founder Sheikh Hamad bin Ali bin Jabr al-Thani suddenly late last year.
Since then it has brought in a new management team.
Qatar Airways has taken its two Boeing 747s out of scheduled service and plans to lease them as charters, leaving four Boeing 727s and two leased Airbus A300-600s on scheduled flights.
Its main competitor is another airline in which the Doha government has a stake -- Gulf Air.

The regional carrier, 25 percent owned by Qatar, operates 150 flights a week out of Doha compared to 80 by Qatar Airways, Hewitt said. Another hurdle is that Qatar Airways has no flying rights to Bahrain -- one of its partners in Gulf Air.
